# Siemens and SAP AI Investment Strategy Comparison

The retrieved excerpts provide substantial detail on SAP's AI investment strategy but only limited information on Siemens' AI approach.

## SAP's AI Investment Strategy

SAP positions itself as "the #1 enterprise application and Business AI company" and frames AI investment as central to its entire business transformation (SAP 2024, p.8). The company commits to "significantly increase our AI investments" in 2025, deploying "nearly 40,000 developers working to deliver an AI-first portfolio and customer experience" (SAP 2024, p.8). SAP sets a specific productivity target: making "every Joule user 30% more efficient by the end of 2025" (SAP 2024, p.8).

The company articulates a comprehensive "AI-First, Suite-First strategy" where AI is "not just adding AI capabilities to existing business processes, but adapting our approach to product development" (SAP 2025, p.41). This involves embedding "Business AI in every application and business process to boost customer productivity, profitability, and innovation" (SAP 2025, p.41). Core elements include Joule (the AI user experience layer), Joule Agents (autonomous AI systems that execute workflows), and SAP Business Data Cloud as the data foundation fueling AI capabilities (SAP 2025, p.42).

SAP positions AI as reshaping the entire enterprise technology market, stating that "business process execution is shifting from individual applications to an agentic AI layer that runs all critical processes and becomes the new user experience" (SAP 2025, p.42). For 2026, the focus intensifies further, including "deploying Joule as the new AI user experience for every user; embedding agentic AI into end-to-end business processes to deliver value through AI assistants" (SAP 2025, p.43).

The company offers "a range of AI-powered use cases built into core business processes across cloud ERP and finance, supply chain, procurement, human resources (HR), sales, marketing and commerce, as well as in IT and across industries, which are used by more than 30,000 customers" (SAP 2024, p.52). In 2025, SAP "released 30 Joule Agents" (SAP 2025, p.43).

SAP's AI governance includes an AI Ethics Steering Committee, with "860 use cases were assessed" in 2025, of which "44% of all relevant use cases were recognized as high risk and reviewed" (SAP 2025, p.194).

## Siemens' AI Investment Strategy

The excerpts provide minimal detail on Siemens' AI investment strategy. The only reference notes that within Digital Industries, "the software business likewise increased revenue, profit and profitability, benefiting from the need for digitalization and strong demand for semiconductor design and AI" (Siemens 2024, p.20). Additionally, Siemens announced at the beginning of fiscal 2025 that it "signed an agreement to acquire Altair Engineering Inc., U.S., a provider of computational science and artificial intelligence software" with the transaction "expected to close in the course of calendar 2025" (Siemens 2024, p.20).

## Key Differences

**Strategic centrality**: SAP frames AI as core to its entire business model transformation and competitive positioning, while the Siemens excerpts mention AI primarily as one market driver among several (electrification, digitalization, decarbonization) and as part of a software acquisition.

**Investment specificity**: SAP provides concrete targets (40,000 developers, 30% efficiency gains, 30 agents released, 860 use cases assessed), while the Siemens excerpts contain no comparable AI investment metrics.

**Product integration depth**: SAP describes comprehensive integration across its entire portfolio with a dedicated AI experience layer (Joule), whereas the Siemens excerpts do not describe AI product integration.

**Governance structure**: SAP details an elaborate AI ethics governance framework with committees and use case review processes; the Siemens excerpts do not address AI governance.

The excerpts do not permit a balanced comparison, as Siemens' AI strategy may be described elsewhere in sections not retrieved.

# Structural Cost Reduction Programs: Cross-Company Comparison

The retrieved excerpts do not cover this topic for most DAX 40 companies, but three companies disclosed specific structural cost reduction programs:

## Companies with Named Programs

**Infineon** disclosed the most extensive structural improvement program. The company launched its "Step Up" program in 2024, incurring restructuring costs of €140 million that year (Infineon 2024, p.81). The program continued into 2025, generating both restructuring and closure expenses of €139 million (Infineon 2025, p.54) plus impairment losses of €74 million on plant and machinery at its Regensburg site (Infineon 2024, p.81). The program delivered measurable operational benefits: cost of goods sold increased less than volume-driven revenue growth due to "measures initiated in the previous year under the 'Step Up' structural improvement program" (Infineon 2025, p.53). Research and development expenses also showed positive effects from the program despite higher headcount (Infineon 2025, p.53).

**SAP** disclosed a major restructuring program in 2024, recording €3,144 million in restructuring expenses that year (SAP 2025, p.243). The expenses included employee-related benefits such as severance payments and accelerated share-based payment expenses, with restructuring payouts totaling €2.5 billion for full year 2024 (SAP 2025, p.242). Separately, SAP executed a "2025 workforce optimization program," though termination benefits for this initiative were not presented as restructuring expenses (SAP 2025, p.242). In 2025, restructuring expenses dropped dramatically to negative €3 million (SAP 2025, p.243).

**BASF** referenced a "Vision and cost-saving program for the Ludwigshafen Verbund site" that the Supervisory Board discussed during 2025 (BASF 2025, p.439), but provided no financial details or implementation specifics in the excerpts.

## Key Differences

The programs differ sharply in scale and focus. Infineon's multi-year operational program totaled roughly €350 million across two years with targeted site-level actions (Infineon 2024, p.81; Infineon 2025, p.54). SAP's restructuring was concentrated in a single year at ten times the magnitude—over €3 billion primarily for workforce reduction (SAP 2025, p.242). BASF mentioned its program only in governance discussions without quantification (BASF 2025, p.439).

**Mercedes-Benz** and **Bayer** disclosed no structural cost reduction programs in the excerpts provided.
